blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Identify the conditions of demand, explain how a change in each shifts the demand curve, and apply the test separating a shift from a movement along the curve.

blocks.heading: What shifts the curve
blocks.text: The conditions of demand are the influences other than the good's own price: consumers' incomes; the prices of related goods; tastes and preferences; expectations of future prices; and the number of consumers. A change in a condition shifts the whole demand curve: an increase in demand moves it to the right, meaning more is bought at every price, and a decrease in demand moves it to the left.

blocks.heading: A shift worked through
blocks.text: A travel magazine names the Etosha area the region's top destination, and tastes turn towards holidays there. At N$900 a night, Etosha Gate Lodge faced demand for 40 rooms a weekend; after the article, the same N$900 brings demand for 60 rooms. The room price has not changed, so this is an increase in demand: the curve has shifted right, and more rooms are wanted at every price.

blocks.heading: Substitutes and complements
blocks.text: Related goods work in two opposite ways. Substitutes replace one another: when the price of Oshakati Textiles' school shirts rises, parents tend to switch towards shirts imported from Vietnam, and demand for the imported shirts rises. Complements are used together: petrol and a trip to the coast are consumed as one outing, so a rise in the price of petrol tends to lower demand for weekends at Swakopmund. A bakery in Portugal sees the same with its custard tarts and the pastries next door.

blocks.heading: Expectations and the number of buyers
blocks.text:
Two conditions of demand work through timing and headcount rather than through income or taste.

Expectations of future prices. Suppose builders in Oshakati hear that the price of cement is expected to rise by 15% next month. Buying now is cheaper than buying later, so many bring their purchases forward: at today's unchanged price of N$110 a bag, more bags are demanded this month. That is an increase in demand, a rightward shift of the curve, caused by what buyers expect rather than by today's price. The effect also works in reverse: if buyers expect a price to fall, as with a new phone model about to replace the old one, many tend to wait, and current demand decreases. Demand that is pulled forward is often followed by weaker demand once the expected change has happened.

The number of consumers. Market demand adds up the demand of every buyer in the market, so more buyers means more demanded at each price. A town grows when its population rises or when people move in for new work or study; when a new college brings 2 000 students to a town, demand for meals, rooms and transport there increases at every price. The age make-up of the population matters too: a country with more young children demands more school uniforms, while an ageing population, as in Japan, demands more health care. A fall in the number of buyers, as when people leave a town after a mine closes, decreases demand and shifts the curve left.

blocks.heading: Movement or shift?
blocks.text: The test is whether the good's own price changed. A cut in the price of juice slides buyers down an unchanged demand curve - a movement. A rise in consumers' incomes, with the price unchanged, moves the whole curve to the right - a shift. Mixing the two up reverses cause and effect: a shift of demand changes the market price; a price change moves the market along the curve.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: A shift of demand changes the market price once supply is drawn in, which is topic 2.5's work; how strongly quantity responds to price is topic 2.7.
